complementary_findings.finding_a: Supplies the baseline-covariate half: quantifies how much prognostic weight a single MMSE carries by showing that the conversion association of automated hippocampal volumetry does not survive adjustment for it (whole-brain volume was not associated with conversion even unadjusted), while also showing that the same volumetry keeps its association with annual CDR-SB change - i.e. it identifies both the problem and the endpoint switch that resolves it.
complementary_findings.finding_b: Supplies the repeated-measure half: three instruments tracked in the same 100 patients over the same 18 months, showing the MMSE registering the smallest proportional decline of the three and the memory-specific RAVLT the largest.
complementary_findings.combined_insight: The MMSE behaves asymmetrically across the two roles a memory service gives it, and the asymmetry works against the service in both directions. WHAT A SHOWS: in 156 memory-clinic patients with subjective cognitive decline or MCI (Oslo), a single baseline MMSE is strong enough that NeuroQuant automated hippocampal volumetry retains no independent association with conversion beside it (whole-brain volume was not associated with conversion even before adjustment) - 'neither remained significantly associated with conversion after adjusting for MMSE-NR' - while the same volumetric measures DO stay associated with annual change in CDR-SB, unadjusted and adjusted. WHAT B ADDS: in 100 post-ischemic-stroke MCI patients (Romania) given three instruments at the same visits over 18 months, the MMSE is the least responsive of the three to real deterioration: MMSE -8.7%, MoCA -10.0%, RAVLT -29.5% (p<0.0001 all), from baselines of MMSE 25.41, MoCA 23.27 and RAVLT 33.63. WHAT THE COMBINATION REVEALS THAT NEITHER SHOWS ALONE: a single instrument is simultaneously the reason an adjunct marker fails to earn its place at baseline and the reason subsequent deterioration is under-registered. An MMSE-centred pathway therefore does two damaging things at once that neither study can see on its own - it sets a baseline covariate stringent enough to null out the incremental value of a candidate marker, and then, as the repeated measure, it under-reports the very decline that marker was bought to anticipate. P-1097 supplies the escape route the pair identifies: switch the follow-up endpoint from the screening score to a staging measure (annual CDR-SB) and the volumetric marker recovers a significant association. CLINICAL IMPLICATION: in memory services that use the MMSE for both triage and monitoring, (a) a null incremental-value result for an imaging or volumetry adjunct, obtained with MMSE in the model, is not evidence that the adjunct is clinically useless - it is partly an artefact of which covariate the service happens to collect first; and (b) a flat serial MMSE in a patient already stratified as high risk is not evidence of stability. Progression monitoring in MCI should be keyed to a staging instrument such as CDR-SB or a memory-specific test, not to the screening score used to enter the pathway.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: In memory services that use the MMSE for both triage and monitoring: (a) a null incremental-value result for an imaging or volumetry adjunct obtained with MMSE in the model is not by itself evidence that the adjunct is clinically useless - in P-1097 the same volumetric measures kept their association with annual CDR-SB change in both unadjusted and adjusted analyses; and (b) a flat serial MMSE in a patient already stratified as high risk is not evidence of stability - in P-1117 the MMSE registered the smallest proportional 18-month decline of three instruments (-8.7% vs MoCA -10.0% and RAVLT -29.5%, p<0.0001 all, from baselines of MMSE 25.41, MoCA 23.27 and RAVLT 33.63). Progression monitoring in MCI should therefore be keyed to a staging instrument such as CDR-SB or a memory-specific test rather than to the screening score used to enter the pathway.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 1): MMSE both suppresses adjunct imaging value at baseline and under-registers longitudinal decline. Evaluation: Caveats noted (note only): the adjusted null is equally consistent with collinearity or power as with genuine absorption; the -8.7%/-29.5% contrast is partly arithmetic (MMSE near its 30-point ceiling vs RAVLT's larger dynamic range); post-ischemic-stroke MCI responsiveness may not transfer to the degenerative memory-clinic population.
complementary_findings.verifier_note_moved_from_clinical_implic: The shared construct is not a design field but a single named instrument measured in both studies - the MMSE - examined in its two distinct clinical roles. Independence is clean: Oslo University Hospital memory clinic (Norway, SCD/MCI, structural MRI) versus the IHCNP study (Romania, post-ischemic-stroke MCI, paper-and-pencil battery); different groups, datasets, countries, modalities and designs, and neither block cites the other. The pair-only clause - that the same instrument suppresses adjunct-marker adoption at baseline and hides decline afterwards - is a pathway-level failure mode that neither paper states or could state. It is also actionably resolvable rather than merely diagnostic, because P-1097 itself contains the counterfactual endpoint (CDR-SB) on which the marker survives.
complementary_findings.audit_note_2026_09_14: Audit 2026-09-14 (UPHOLD_WITH_NOTES, major). (1) clinical_implication contained verifier meta-commentary ('The shared construct is not a design field...') rather than a clinical implication - the batch caveat_summary lists 'meta-commentary implication swaps' as a mandated revision class. The clinical guidance already present inside combined_insight was moved into clinical_implication (restated with block numbers); the displaced meta-commentary is preserved verbatim in verifier_note_moved_from_clinical_implication_2026_09_14. (2) WBV phrasing corrected per P-1097 line 160080 ('Hippocampus volume, but not WBV, was associated with conversion ... but neither remained significantly associated with conversion after adjusting for MMSE-NR. Both hippocampus volume and WBV were associated with progression measured by annual change in CDR-SB, in both unadjusted and adjusted analyses'). P-1117 numbers per line 161908 ('MMSE 25.41, MoCA 23.27, RAVLT 33.63 ... MMSE -8.7%, MoCA -10.0%, RAVLT -29.5% (p<0.0001 all)'), population per line 161905 ('100 patients with MCI after ischemic stroke (Romania)'). The operator's collinearity/power caveat is not block-derivable and stays note-only. Status kept.

complementary_findings.finding_a: Supplies the mirror. An independent cohort (AIBL, Australia), an unrelated exposure, and a protective-direction estimate of comparable magnitude on the same CDR-SOB units/year scale, from a cohort whose stated entry rule removes recently diagnosed cancer patients. It never measures pre-exposure slope, so it cannot see in itself what P-1216 measured in itself.
complementary_findings.finding_b: Supplies the demonstration. In an amyloid-stratified ADNI cohort with IPTW and time-varying Cox modelling, reports the harmful-direction estimate AND the LOESS observation that cognitive decline began before ChEI initiation, which is the only direct within-study measurement in the pair of a slope difference that predates the exposure. Its own problems section names indication bias explicitly.
complementary_findings.combined_insight: Two independent observational MCI cohorts report exposure effects on the SAME instrument - annualised CDR-SB/CDR-SOB change - that are of comparable magnitude and opposite sign, and in each case the cohort's own entry or allocation rule points in exactly the direction of the reported effect. P-1216 (ADNI, 558 amnestic MCI) reports cholinesterase-inhibitor users declining 0.35 CDR-SB units/year faster with progression HR 1.77, and supplies the decisive within-study observation that the decline began BEFORE ChEI initiation, i.e. the exposed group was already on the steeper slope before the exposure existed. P-1204 (AIBL, 2136 participants) reports the mirror image - cancer history associated with a 0.23 units/year SLOWER annualised CDR-SOB and a halved MCI-to-AD progression risk (RR 0.50) - from a cohort whose own limitation section records that AIBL excludes participants with cancer in the past 5 years, a filter that removes the sickest exposed patients but whose slope consequence is never measured. What the pair reveals and neither shows alone: P-1216 empirically demonstrates that non-random entry into an exposure group produces a CDR-SB slope difference of the same order as the effect being attributed to the exposure, and P-1204 shows the identical order of slope difference arising in the opposite direction in a cohort with a documented but unquantified entry filter. P-1216 has only the harmful direction and P-1204 never measures pre-exposure slope, so neither can calibrate its own estimate against this.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: Bears on two live prescribing and counselling decisions in amnestic MCI. P-1216 explicitly argues its result 'calls for critical re-evaluation of ChEI prescription practices in MCI'; P-1204's result would, if taken at face value, reassure a cancer survivor presenting with MCI that their conversion risk is halved. The pair says that an observational exposure-progression signal of roughly 0.2-0.35 CDR-SB units per year in an MCI cohort is at the magnitude that the cohort's own selection into the exposed group has been shown to generate, so neither signal is strong enough to withdraw a cholinesterase inhibitor from a patient who reports benefit, nor to alter the prognosis given to a cancer survivor with MCI. The decision-grade version of either question requires a design that measures pre-exposure slope (P-1216 has the method; P-1204 does not) or randomises the exposure.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 1): Same CDR decline metric shows opposite exposure associations while each cohort contains an explicit selection mechanism. Evaluation: Source anomaly noted: the quoted 'HR=1.77, CI 1.15-2.73, p=0.001' is internally inconsistent (that CI implies p~0.01) - verify against P-1216 before citing; 'cancer history and ChEI are biologically unrelated exposures' objection and measured-vs-argued asymmetry noted.
complementary_findings.audit_note_2026_09_14: Audit 2026-09-14 (CHALLENGE, critical) claimed the P-1204 entry-filter clause 'appears NOWHERE in the P-1204 block'. On re-read this is refuted: the block's '### Potential gaps or limitations' section, line 171294, reads 'AIBL excludes participants with cancer in the past 5 years (selection bias)' (the audit checked only the '### What are the problems?' section at line 171230). The P-1204 PDF (downloads/2. Animal Models and Pre-clinical Mechanisms/PMID_38388558_41598_2024_Article_54875.pdf) limitations paragraph states verbatim: 'the AIBL study excludes participants who had cancer in the past 5 years from recruitment (excluding skin or in situ prostate cancer), which can potentially contribute to selection bias', so the block is faithful to the paper and the record's clause is supported. Only change: 'anyone' -> 'participants' to match the block wording. NOT demoted: the demotion instruction was premised on the refuted finding; the operator's ACCEPT and human_evaluation_note stand untouched. Operator may wish to add the PDF's skin/in-situ-prostate exception to the block if re-summarising.

complementary_findings.finding_a: Empirical arm. Delivers a near-deterministic risk separation at both extremes of the amyloid-elevated MCI stratum using clinic-available instruments, proposes memory-clinic stratification and trial enrichment as the use case, and reports no discrimination metric - the quantity P-1171's model consumes.
complementary_findings.finding_b: Evaluative arm. The only paper here that models the downstream decision rather than measuring discrimination: it prices the act of risk disclosure, finds current practice dominant in the no-treatment base case, and identifies sensitivity/specificity, treatment-eligibility proportion and disutility-of-prognosis as the value drivers - with tool performance an assumed, not measured, input.
complementary_findings.combined_insight: The empirical and the evaluative halves of the MCI risk-stratification question cannot currently be joined, and each paper holds exactly the half the other is missing. P-1226 supplies an extreme empirical separation built from instruments a memory clinic already runs - Cog_Vol, a hippocampal-volume-to-ADAS13 ratio, splits PET-amyloid-elevated MCI into 94.1% two-year conversion and 0 of 42 four-year conversion - but reports it as within-stratum conversion rates and explicitly reports no AUC, sensitivity or specificity. P-1171 supplies the only decision model, and finds that at an ASSUMED 95% sensitivity/specificity over a 5-year horizon with no treatment available, current practice DOMINATES risk prediction (9.36 vs 9.32 QALYs at lower cost), because the disutility of receiving a high-risk prognosis outweighs the benefit of a low-risk one. The pair reveals two things neither paper contains: first, the strongest empirical stratifier in this batch does not report the quantity the only value model needs as its input, so the two literatures are not commensurable even in principle as written; second, the very use P-1226 proposes - disclosing a 94.1% two-year conversion risk to a memory-clinic patient - is precisely the event P-1171 models as a COST, and P-1171's verdict says the binding constraint on deployment is the absence of an action to take on the result, not the quality of the marker.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: Names the implementation decision a memory clinic actually faces: whether to compute and disclose an ADAS13-plus-hippocampal-volume risk stratum to an amyloid-positive MCI patient in a setting where no disease-modifying treatment is available to that patient. P-1226 proposes exactly this use ('providing an easy tool for memory-clinic risk stratification and clinical-trial enrichment'). P-1171's model returns negative net health for that act under its base case, and identifies treatment eligibility and the disutility of risk disclosure - not discrimination - as the drivers of value. For a clinic, the pair says the prerequisite for adopting a cheap MCI stratifier is a defined downstream action (trial enrolment, a treatable comorbidity, an accessible therapy), and that the field's continued investment in better markers does not relieve that prerequisite. It also names the concrete closure step: report sensitivity and specificity (or a c-index) alongside the stratum conversion rates, because without them no empirical MCI stratifier in this batch can be evaluated by the only value model in it.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 2): Empirical stratification and decision-utility modelling supply complementary halves of deployment, but metrics are not commensurate. Evaluation: Reversibility caveat (dominance rests on a single parameter with no probabilistic sensitivity analysis) and in-sample cut-off tuning carried; kept despite the residual's 'withdraw in favour of conv-01' alternative - decision-model arms are exactly what the corpus lacks.

complementary_findings.finding_a: Supplies the barrier taxonomy from the non-engaging side (26 community-dwelling MCI adults across four provinces, recruited outside any programme), and the completer-adherence benchmark (~60-65%) that frames adherence as a retention problem.
complementary_findings.finding_b: Supplies the stage structure (Multi-Theory Model: 6 initiation subthemes vs 5 maintenance subthemes, 20 patients recruited from a tertiary hospital plus community screening) and the uptake denominator (~2% participation) that reframes the same problem as a recruitment problem.
complementary_findings.combined_insight: MCI lifestyle-programme non-adherence is two different behaviours with non-overlapping determinants, and the dominant loss is never-starting rather than dropping out. P-1123 characterises why community-dwelling MCI adults do not engage in self-management at all - misperception of MCI risk and personal control, elder self-neglect, and absent information/support services - treating engagement as one construct. P-1170 ADDS the stage split: it partitions the same behaviour into initiation drivers (perceived disease threat, cognitive anosognosia, access and cost barriers) and maintenance drivers (in-programme experience, self-regulation, family/peer/professional supervision, high time preference, frailty), and contrasts participation as low as ~2% against the ~60-65% completer-adherence figure that motivates P-1123; both figures are background citations over different denominators (people eligible for a multidomain intervention vs people enrolled in a structured programme), so the 'the loss is at uptake' conclusion rests on the qualitative stage assignment rather than a single measured funnel. Combined, the two locate P-1123's perception barrier specifically at initiation and its support-service barrier specifically at maintenance, and place the larger numeric loss at the pre-enrolment stage that neither paper measures on its own.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: For services commissioning MCI lifestyle or self-management programmes in Chinese community and memory-clinic settings, the dominant loss point is pre-enrolment, not attrition. The screening-to-referral pathway therefore needs a risk-perception and anosognosia component delivered BEFORE enrolment (targeting the patients P-1123 interviewed, who are never in a programme to be counted), while family, peer and professional-supervision supports are what keep enrolled patients in. A programme audited on completer adherence will report 60-65% success while reaching a small minority of eligible patients, so uptake among screened-positive patients - not completion - is the metric that should govern whether the service is working.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 1): Two studies identify initiation versus maintenance barriers within the same adherence problem. Evaluation: The ~2%-vs-60-65% magnitude claim bounded in-insight: both figures are background citations over different denominators (eligible for a multidomain intervention vs enrolled in a structured programme), so 'the loss is at uptake' rests on the qualitative stage assignment; uptake-not-completion implication retained.
complementary_findings.operator_caveat: Operator G4 required this caveat to appear as an explicit limitation in the manuscript text, not as a quality-flag footnote; the combined_insight / clinical_implication / human_evaluation_note above already carry it.

complementary_findings.finding_a: whole-food anthocyanin arm: PRISMA review of berry polyphenols with structured risk-of-bias assessment showing consistent preclinical mechanisms and directionally positive but inconclusive human cognitive effects, blocked at trial quality and standardisation
complementary_findings.finding_b: isolated-compound arm: narrative review of punicalagin showing preclinical mechanisms across five MCI models and human translation blocked at bioavailability and gut-metabolite exposure
complementary_findings.combined_insight: Two independent reviews of polyphenol interventions relevant to MCI reach converging translation-deficit verdicts from different compounds: P-1172 (berries/anthocyanins) finds human-trial evidence limited and inconclusive despite favourable direction, with 12 of 13 included human trials at some-concerns risk of bias; P-1176 (punicalagin/pomegranate) finds preclinical mechanism positive but human translation absent, with low oral bioavailability (18.17%) and extensive gut metabolism named as the key barrier and no large RCT existing. Across the compounds these two reviews cover, the preclinical-positive / human-evidence-absent pattern recurs with compound-specific failure points (trial quality and dose standardisation for berries; exposure mismatch and no large RCT for punicalagin); two compounds cannot establish that the pattern is structural to the polyphenol class as a whole, and P-1176 is overclaim-flagged for its own positive framing.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: Polyphenol-based nutraceuticals for MCI are not supported by direct human evidence in either review: the two reviews identify different blocking steps for different compound types (trial quality and dose standardisation for berries/anthocyanins; exposure mismatch - 18.17% oral bioavailability with gut metabolism - and no large RCT for punicalagin) that converge on the same absent human endpoint, so dietary counselling should not present them as an MCI treatment pending human trials that co-measure cognition and exposure; two compounds cannot establish that the pattern is structural to the polyphenol class as a whole.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 2): Two reviews converge on translational limitations across compounds, but evidence remains review-level and caveated. Evaluation: Class-level implication contradiction fixed (two compounds cannot establish a class-level pattern; corpus papers P-873 EVOO and P-875 GSPE could test it); review-pairing flag noted; meta-commentary implication replaced with guidance.
complementary_findings.operator_caveat: Operator G4 required this caveat to appear as an explicit limitation in the manuscript text, not as a quality-flag footnote; the combined_insight / clinical_implication / human_evaluation_note above already carry it.

complementary_findings.finding_a: supplies the upstream arm: Medicare claims O/E analysis across 226,756 clinicians quantifying how rarely MCI is diagnosed relative to expected prevalence
complementary_findings.finding_b: supplies the downstream arm: dyadic decision-factor study of 65 referred patients and study partners quantifying what drives biomarker-testing decisions after specialist referral
complementary_findings.combined_insight: P-858 quantifies the upstream MCI detection bottleneck in US primary care (detection rate 0.08 against expectation; 99.9% of 226,756 clinicians significantly below expected diagnosis; over a quarter of panels with zero diagnosed MCI - with the caveat that a demographics-only expected model cannot fully separate genuine low-prevalence panels from under-detection), while P-857 characterises the downstream post-referral decision environment in a single academic dementia-specialist clinic (35.4% of 65 referred patients already biomarker-tested; clinical utility and clinician recommendation rated most important, while cost of testing and health-insurance implications were - in the paper's own hedge - 'not rated as highly important factors'; the printed patient-side minimum was fear of testing procedures (3.33) and the partner-side minimum health-insurance concern (3.70), and no mean for cost of the test is printed). The two ends of the MCI diagnosis pathway have been measured by different studies with different failure modes - near-total upstream non-detection at system level, and a downstream referral process in which economic factors were not among the highly rated decision factors - but the downstream evidence comes from one specialist sample (87.7% White non-Hispanic, mean 16.8 years of education) that cannot represent primary-care decision-making, so the pair contrasts two different settings rather than two stages of one pathway, and no study connects the two ends.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: For policy and service design, the pair locates the binding constraint at the detection end, not the referral end: P-858 shows near-total under-diagnosis in US primary care (99.9% of 226,756 clinicians significantly below expected MCI diagnosis), while P-857 suggests the specialist end, in this sample, was not dominated by economic concerns (cost of testing and insurance implications were 'not rated as highly important factors', though fear of testing was the patients' lowest-rated factor and no cost mean is printed), so on this evidence detection and outreach interventions are the more strongly indicated lever, with the case against financing reform at the referral stage resting on the paper's hedge rather than on a ranking; the downstream evidence is a single academic-centre sample (87.7% White non-Hispanic, mean 16.8 years of education) and cannot represent primary care, so the upstream/downstream contrast is between two different settings, not two stages of one pathway.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 2): System-level detection bottleneck and specialist-clinic decision environment are complementary pathway stages. Evaluation: Settings-vs-stages bound added (academic-specialist dyads vs primary care; P-857's sample is 87.7% White non-Hispanic, mean 16.8 years of education); 'detection rate 0.08' computation basis (panel-level vs clinician-level means ~0.053) unstated - noted; guidance written for the implication.
complementary_findings.operator_caveat: Operator G4 required this caveat to appear as an explicit limitation in the manuscript text, not as a quality-flag footnote; the combined_insight / clinical_implication / human_evaluation_note above already carry it.
complementary_findings.audit_note_2026_09_14: Audit 2026-09-14 (CHALLENGE, major): the record upgraded P-857's hedge into a ranking ('cost and insurance lowest' / 'rank last'). P-857 block line 129944/130056 quotes the paper: 'cost of testing and implications to health insurance were not rated as highly important factors'; line 129930: 'The factor with the lowest mean importance rating for patients was fear of testing procedures (3.33, 95% CI: 3.02, 3.66) while for partners it was concerns that the result may affect health insurance (3.70, 95% CI: 3.25, 4.16)' and 'Mean importance ratings for the other four factors - cost of the test ... are not printed'; line 130056: 'The hedge is the ceiling here and must not be upgraded into a ranking'. Wording reverted to the hedge in combined_insight and clinical_implication; the policy conclusion softened accordingly. P-858 figures verified at lines 130482-130484 (0.08; 226,518 of 226,756 = 99.9%; 'Over a quarter'). Status kept.

complementary_findings.finding_a: supplies the deployment-ready model: large-scale EHR conversion prediction at AUC 0.73 with calibration (Brier 0.18) on held-out data
complementary_findings.finding_b: supplies the disclosure-cost arm: DCE/TTO valuation showing asymmetric utility impact of receiving high (-0.18) versus low (+0.06) predicted risk
complementary_findings.combined_insight: P-1081 demonstrates a deployable 5-year MCI-to-dementia conversion model from routine EHR data (AUC 0.73, 95% CI 0.72-0.74, 59,782 veterans, held-out evaluation; with unexplained protective associations for high BMI, alcohol abuse and sleep apnoea), while P-1075 measures, in hypothetical valuations by a Dutch general-population sample, that a health state labelled high predicted dementia risk carries -0.18 utility versus +0.06 for low risk. Read together, the corpus holds a scale-deployable conversion model and a measured-stated-preference asymmetry suggesting high-risk labels carry net utility cost for the labelled person - but the utility estimates are hypothetical valuations in a different population, not observed post-disclosure outcomes, no evidence ties the model's operating range to the harm range, and P-1075's own open problem is precisely that real-disclosure utility change is unmeasured. The pair prices a deployment tension that model papers do not price; it does not establish the harm.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: Before deploying MCI-to-dementia risk prediction, decision-makers should weigh that disclosure carries a modelled utility cost for most labelled patients (-0.18 for a high-risk label vs +0.06 for low risk; hypothetical valuations in a Dutch general-population sample, not observed post-disclosure outcomes) while the treatment availability that would mitigate that cost is exactly what the deployable model (P-1081, AUC 0.73 on 59,782 veterans) cannot supply; the pair prices the deployment tension but does not establish the harm, so real-disclosure utility measurement is the prerequisite evidence.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 2): Risk-model utility tension is real, although the downstream economic harm remains modelled rather than directly observed. Evaluation: Meta-commentary implication replaced with guidance; reversibility and in-sample tuning caveats noted.

complementary_findings.finding_a: PROSPERO-registered qualitative evidence synthesis (11 studies, 4,706 records screened) of older adults' experience of receiving an MCI diagnosis: two-sided redeemed/isolated response, label confusion, fear from conflation with dementia, lack of follow-up care feeding uncertainty and distress
complementary_findings.finding_b: Cross-sectional survey of 116 physician-diagnosed MCI/mild-dementia patients in two Taiwanese teaching hospitals measuring advance-care-planning engagement: 42.2 percent high intention to attend ACP consultation, 8.6 percent signed a living will, 6.0 percent DNR, 0.9 percent healthcare agent, with knowledge measures dropping out of both multivariate models
complementary_findings.combined_insight: P-696 synthesises how receiving an MCI diagnosis is experienced (a two-sided 'redeemed or isolated' response, with absent post-diagnostic support feeding uncertainty and distress), and P-697 measures what engagement with future planning actually looks like immediately downstream (42.2 percent high intention to attend ACP consultation, 8.6 percent having signed a living will, knowledge scores not retained as predictors). Together they reveal a consecutive-stage breakdown in the same post-diagnostic pathway: the review shows the diagnosis is delivered without support, and the survey shows that when support-adjacent decisions arrive, fewer than half intend to engage and under one in ten have documented anything - so the communication failure P-696 locates at disclosure is visible again as an engagement failure at care planning, and neither stage's evidence can be produced by the other's methods.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: Post-diagnostic care for newly diagnosed MCI should pair the disclosure itself with structured, supported care-planning: the diagnosis is experienced as two-sided ('redeemed or isolated') with absent post-diagnostic support feeding uncertainty and distress (P-696), and downstream advance-care-planning engagement is low (42.2% high intention to attend ACP consultation; 8.6% living will) with knowledge scores not retained as predictors (P-697) - consistent with information provision without supported deliberation not converting into planning.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 2): Diagnosis-experience evidence and advance-care-planning uptake expose adjacent post-diagnostic failures. Evaluation: Meta-commentary implication replaced with guidance; the review-survey stage pairing is directional and the promoted text preserves that scoping.

complementary_findings.finding_a: meta-analysis of VR-wrapped combined cognitive-physical intervention RCTs in older adults with MCI: significant pooled effect on global cognition only, with explicit nulls on memory and executive function/attention and a decline to run the VR-vs-no-VR comparison that would isolate the VR ingredient
complementary_findings.finding_b: diagnostic-test-accuracy meta-analysis of 14 studies pooling VR-based cognitive tests against clinical reference standards for MCI detection, with pooled sensitivity 0.89 (95% CI 0.82-0.94)
complementary_findings.combined_insight: The corpus splits VR's two proposed roles in MCI, with the assessment arm weaker than its headline: as a therapy wrapper, a meta-analysis of VR-wrapped combined cognitive-physical RCTs in older adults with MCI found a significant pooled effect on global cognition only, conceded nulls on memory and executive function/attention, and declined the VR-vs-no-VR comparison that would isolate VR as the active ingredient - so the ingredient role is untested, not measured absent (P-833); as a diagnostic instrument, a meta-analysis of 14 studies reports VR-based tests with pooled sensitivity 0.89 (95% CI 0.82-0.94) against clinical reference standards, framed by its authors as comparable or better than paper-and-pencil screening - but that pooled estimate carries severe unexplained heterogeneity (I-squared 0.81/0.87), a threshold effect over study-selected cut-offs, 178 double-counted individuals across 14 study-rows in 13 reports, and internally irreconcilable participant/case totals, making it an optimistic upper bound rather than a transportable screening performance (P-836). Read together: VR's assessment use case has pooled evidence whose strength is uncertain, and its treatment-ingredient use case has never been isolated; neither review's design can produce the other's result.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: For procurement and clinical use, VR in MCI currently supports an assessment-instrument claim (pooled sensitivity 0.89, 95% CI 0.82-0.94, against clinical reference standards - though an optimistic upper bound given severe heterogeneity, threshold effects and double-counted participants) and does not support a treatment-ingredient claim (VR-wrapped combined interventions improved global cognition only, with the VR-vs-no-VR comparison never run); services should not buy VR as a therapy until the ingredient is isolated, and any screening estimate should be treated conservatively.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 2): Genuine methodological pair; heterogeneity/double-counting mean any pooled performance interpretation must be conservative. Evaluation: Meta-commentary implication replaced with guidance (assessment claim supported-but-conservative; treatment-ingredient claim never isolated); shared authorship across arms (Mingli Yan) and the genre-difference alternative noted.

complementary_findings.finding_a: mini review of 9 human probiotic studies (4 MCI, 2 healthy older adults, 3 AD): all four MCI studies improved cognition, but the review's own limitation register states no gut-related parameters were measured in any MCI or AD study, and several MCI studies confounded probiotics with fermented soybean or exercise co-interventions
complementary_findings.finding_b: narrative review of pomegranate polyphenol punicalagin for MCI: preclinical efficacy across five rodent models, four mechanisms consolidated, oral bioavailability 18.17 percent, gut metabolism to ellagic acid/urolithins with three metabotypes, no large RCT in MCI
complementary_findings.combined_insight: P-1198 shows that all four human probiotic studies in MCI reported improved cognitive function while no MCI or AD study measured any gut-related parameter, so the proposed gut-microbiota mechanism of the cognitive benefit is entirely untested in the very studies that claim it. P-1176 adds the pharmacokinetic half of the same translation problem from a different intervention class: punicalagin's cognitive effects are established in preclinical models while its oral bioavailability is only 18.17 percent with extensive gut metabolism, so the compound tested in animals is largely not the compound circulating in humans. Together they reveal a common structural failure in MCI nutraceutical intervention research: in one case the mechanism is never measured in humans despite positive cognition results, in the other the active human exposure is never demonstrated despite preclinical mechanisms - the mechanism-to-human-translation link is missing at both ends.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: MCI nutraceutical trials should be required to measure the proposed mechanism in humans: the gut-microbiome mechanism of probiotic cognitive benefit has never been measured in any MCI/AD study despite positive cognition results (P-1198), and punicalagin's active human exposure is not demonstrated (oral bioavailability 18.17%, metabotype-dependent gut metabolism) despite strong preclinical mechanisms (P-1176) - no human measurement connects either intervention to its proposed mechanism.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 1): Human probiotic cognition evidence plus preclinical punicalagin PK failure gives a clear two-sided translation gap. Evaluation: Meta-commentary implication replaced with guidance; both arms' failure modes documented (mechanism never measured in humans; active exposure never demonstrated).

complementary_findings.finding_a: ADNI practice-effect quantification: PE adjustment increased MCI prevalence at follow-up by 9.2 percent (272 vs 249), reduced reversion by 28.8 percent (57 vs 80 reverters), doubled dementia HR, and 72.2 percent of false reverters were amyloid/tau-positive
complementary_findings.finding_b: Taipei Veterans General Hospital memory-clinic cohort (418 MCI + 146 NC, ADNI2 EMCI/LMCI criteria): first-year reversion 54/161 EMCI (32.8 percent) versus 16/258 LMCI (5 percent), with EMCI reverters indistinguishable from NC in subsequent survival and LMCI reverters still at higher decline risk
complementary_findings.combined_insight: P-971 shows that cognitive practice effects manufacture apparent MCI reversion (PE adjustment cuts 1-year reverters 80 to 57, a 28.8 percent reduction, doubles the dementia hazard ratio of the MCI diagnosis, and 72.2 percent of the removed false reverters are positive for at least one amyloid/tau biomarker), while P-975 shows that genuine reversion is strongly stage-dependent (first-year reversion 32.8 percent in EMCI versus 5 percent in LMCI, with EMCI reverters matching normal controls on dementia-free survival while LMCI reverters remain at elevated risk). Together they separate the two components the reversion literature conflates: a measurement artefact (practice effects inflating apparent reversion, removable by statistical adjustment and partly biomarker-confirmed as misclassification) and a real clinical signal (stage-graded reversion in early disease), each invisible without the other's correction - a reversion rate adjusted for practice effects but not for stage, or staged but not practice-corrected, is not interpretable.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: Reversion figures should be read as interpretable only after both practice-effect correction and stage stratification: P-971 quantifies the practice-effect artefact share (a 28.8% reduction in apparent reverters, 72.2% of the removed false reverters biomarker-positive) and P-975 the stage gradient (a 6.5-fold EMCI-vs-LMCI difference), so the corpus's existing frequency claims (VF-33's 30-48%) are upper bounds, and an uncorrected or unstaged first-year reversion figure must not drive de-escalation or discharge decisions.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 1): Practice-artifact evidence and stage-dependent reversion cleanly separate two explanations of apparent recovery. Evaluation: Meta-commentary implication replaced with guidance (reversion rates interpretable only after both corrections; VF-33's 30-48% claims are upper bounds).

complementary_findings.finding_a: 1:3 propensity-matched Merative MarketScan claims study, 20,740 adults 50+: 25 comorbidities significantly associated with MCI, ORs and AUC decaying monotonically with age, best BLLR model AUC 0.72 on a 30 percent hold-out
complementary_findings.finding_b: four-year repeated-measures GEE study of 93 amnestic-MCI outpatients (Winblad criteria, CDR 0.5): comorbidity severity predicts faster CDR-SB progression, metabolic domain rho = 0.41, baseline physical activity protective interaction with time
complementary_findings.combined_insight: Comorbidity's clinical role appears to invert across the MCI disease course, on evidence from two disjoint designs: in a 1:3 propensity-matched US claims study (20,740 adults 50+), 25 comorbidities associate significantly with MCI but both the odds ratios (depression 4.4/3.1/2.9; stroke/TIA 6.4/3.0/2.1 across 50-64/65-79/80+) and model discrimination (AUC 0.75/0.70/0.66) weaken monotonically with age - a detection signal strongest where MCI is youngest (P-1067); within established MCI, a four-year GEE study of 93 amnestic-MCI outpatients shows comorbidity severity significantly accelerates CDR-SB progression (metabolic domain rho = 0.41) while baseline physical activity buffers decline - a prognostic signal once MCI is established (P-1065). Neither paper states or could test the other's endpoint, so the inversion is a cross-study structural reading, not a within-cohort demonstration; a possible mechanism for the age-decay (comorbidity becoming ubiquitous among progressors) is hypothesised and untested. The same variable plausibly belongs in young-old screening models and in MCI prognosis plans, for different reasons and with different age gradients.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: Comorbidity data should be age-banded in MCI detection models (the detection signal weakens monotonically with age: AUC 0.75/0.70/0.66 across 50-64/65-79/80+, P-1067) and treated as a modifiable prognostic factor once MCI is established (comorbidity severity accelerates CDR-SB progression, metabolic domain rho=0.41, with baseline physical activity protective, P-1065); the inversion is a cross-study structural reading, not a within-cohort demonstration.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 2): Comorbidity behaves differently at MCI detection versus established-disease progression; useful stage-dependent complement. Evaluation: Meta-commentary implication replaced with guidance (age-banded detection models; modifiable prognostic factor in clinic); the inversion is a cross-study structural reading, not a within-cohort demonstration.

complementary_findings.finding_a: PRISMA meta-analysis of 87 prospective cohorts (225,584 participants; meta-analysed subset 44,199) pooling 14 modifiable exposures for incident MCI in baseline-normal elders, with seven significant and seven null pools and the late-life hypertension null explicitly engaged against the Lancet Commission framework
complementary_findings.finding_b: Rush Memory and Aging Project cohort (1,312 dementia-free, 540 autopsies, up to 21 years follow-up, COPD excluded): lowest pulmonary-function tertile HR 1.95 for incident MCI, HR 1.55 for MCI-to-dementia, autopsy AD pathology OR 1.32 and vascular pathology OR 3.05
complementary_findings.combined_insight: P-843 supplies the field's systematic evidence map for modifiable risk factors of incident MCI in cognitively normal older adults - 87 studies, 14 pooled estimates, exactly half significant (diabetes-HR, anxiety-6y, depression-3y/5y, apathy, night-time behaviour, physical frailty) with the other half null (hypertension, diabetes-OR, anxiety-4y, depression-6y, agitation, irritability, eating problems) - and pulmonary function is absent from its pooled exposure set. P-959 supplies the missing exposure from a clinical-pathological cohort: lowest-tertile pulmonary function carries HR 1.95 (95% CI 1.43-2.66) for incident MCI and HR 1.55 (1.03-2.33) for MCI-to-dementia, with autopsy decomposition showing a vascular-pathology channel (OR 3.05) about three times the AD-pathology channel (OR 1.32). Together they reveal a coverage gap in the systematic map: a modifiable organ-system exposure absent from the 14-pool synthesis carries one of the larger single-cohort incident-MCI effect sizes and acts substantially through the vascular pathway - the pathway where the map's most prominent vascular exposure (late-life hypertension) turns null even as its diabetes-HR pool is significant, indicating the map characterises the vascular route incompletely rather than not at all. The effect-size comparison spans different designs and adjustment sets and is illustrative, not like-for-like.
complementary_findings.clinical_implication: Prevention-framework and guideline authors should not rely on cardiometabolic/psychosocial exposure maps alone: pulmonary function is absent from the field's systematic pooled set (P-843's 14 pooled estimates) yet carries HR 1.95 (95% CI 1.43-2.66) for incident MCI and HR 1.55 for MCI-to-dementia, with an autopsy-decomposed vascular channel about three times the AD channel (OR 3.05 vs 1.32, P-959) - so respiratory screening belongs in the incident-MCI risk map; the effect-size comparison spans different designs and adjustment sets and is illustrative, not like-for-like.
complementary_findings.human_evaluation_note: G4 ACCEPT (operator, Tier 2): Systematic mapping omits pulmonary function while independent incidence/progression evidence indicates a coverage gap. Evaluation: Meta-commentary implication replaced with guidance (respiratory screening belongs in the incident-MCI risk map); the effect-size comparison is illustrative, not like-for-like.

complementary_findings.reject_recommended_operator_review_2026_: REJECT RECOMMENDED (recommendation only - NOT applied; status is unchanged and remains pending_human_review). The decisive ground is NOT the construct mismatch alone. GROUND 1 (the stronger one): P-1340 achieves sex parity BECAUSE it fits sex-specific models. Its own block declares 'development of sex-specific SRSS-CNMCI' and 'sex-stratified Cox scoring', and the two C-statistics the record quotes (0.902 female, 0.911 male) come from two SEPARATE models, one fitted per sex. Equal discrimination between two separately-fitted models is a property of the MODELLING CHOICE, not of the marker class. The record's combined_insight nonetheless headlines that 'sex parity in early-cognitive-impairment models depends on the marker class', and concludes that sex-disaggregated reporting is needed 'for molecular panels specifically'. That conclusion is confounded at its root: a single pooled model on P-1340's four clinical predictors has not been shown to achieve parity, and P-1366's panel was not fitted sex-specifically. GROUND 2 (the construct mismatch, real but secondary): P-1340 reports a Cox C-statistic for INCIDENT CN-to-MCI conversion over follow-up (Assigned: T2 prognostic/conversion prediction), while P-1366 reports cross-sectional ROC AUC for AD-vs-control and impaired-vs-control discrimination. These are not the same quantity and are not comparable as 'discrimination'. GROUND 3: four things differ simultaneously between the two papers - marker class, estimand (prognostic C-index vs diagnostic AUC), cohort (ADNI/HABS vs P-1366's series) and model structure (sex-stratified vs pooled) - so no single-factor attribution to sex or to marker class can be isolated from this pair. Note also that grounds 1 and 2 are already written in the record's own review_note; what this field adds is that ground 1, not ground 2, is the one that should carry the decision.

verification_warrant_operator_review_202.written: 2026-09-14 (operator review, CF package). NOT a gate. No CF record was moved to confirmed or rejected in this pass; the operator deliberately held the CF gate back because the criterion that defined the 'gate-ready' set was shown to be unreliable.
verification_warrant_operator_review_202.scope: CF-194..CF-219, 26 records. Every one of the 26 carries a 'verification' object with grounding_ok = true and a method of the form 'claude_adversarial_source_verification against <named sources> (2026-08-26)'. PRECISION NOTE: the method NAME and DATE are identical across all 26; the source arguments differ per record (e.g. CF-196 names pdf_extract_878.txt, CF-215 names pdf_extract_930.txt and the P-803 registry row). The claim 'one identical method string' is true of the method name and date, not of the full string.
verification_warrant_operator_review_202.split: The earlier worklist recorded '16 gate-ready / 22 with no verification trail'. The true split of the 2026-08-29 self-certification revert block (CF-194..CF-245, 52 records, all carrying selfcert_revert_2026_08_29) is 26/26: CF-194..CF-219 carry the 2026-08-26 verification object, CF-220..CF-245 do not. CF-220..CF-245 are not wholly untouched - they carry verified_by (a batch label: actor-critic-manual-* for CF-220..238, manual-source-* for CF-239..245) and review_status = awaiting_human_gate - but they carry no grounding assertion.
demonstrated_false_passes: CF-196: verification.method asserts grounding against pdf_extract_878.txt and grounding_ok = true. pdf_extract_878.txt REFUTES the P-878 block that finding_a is drawn from: the extract enrolled 2431 participants from the 2015 CHARLS wave and contains no occurrence of lavaan, semTools, 5,000 bootstrap replications, CFI, RMSEA, SRMR, SEM or 'structural equation'; the block and CF-196.finding_a assert N=4,262, CHARLS Wave 4 (2018) and all of that machinery. See _quarantine.suspect_papers.

CF-215: verification.method asserts grounding against pdf_extract_930.txt and the P-803 registry record, grounding_ok = true. CF-215.finding_b attributes to P-803 the odds ratios 'OR 1.88 for long sleep + poor sleep quality vs 1.33 with good quality; short sleepers with 30-60 min naps OR 0.72'. Those three figures are P-891's: they occur in the P-891 block (summaries.md L136088ff) 4, 3 and 4 times respectively, and ZERO times in the P-803 block (summaries.md L90346ff). P-803's own reported odds ratios are 2.286, 3.368, 2.733, 2.015, 3.480, 2.132 and 2.013, and P-803 has no sleep-quality measure at all (its effect modifier is metabolic syndrome). CF-215's review_note additionally asserts the pairing is 'distinct and non-overlapping' from CF-199, which is contradicted by its own finding_b carrying CF-199's paper_a's numbers.
verification_warrant_operator_review_202.false_pass_rate: At least 2 of 26 = 7.7 per cent. This is a FLOOR, not an estimate. Both false passes were found BY HAND while working other items in this pass, not by a systematic re-check of the 26. The other 24 records have not been independently re-grounded, so the true rate is unknown and can only be higher or equal.
verification_warrant_operator_review_202.consequence: The presence of a verification block is NOT a sufficient warrant for gating. The block asserts grounding; it does not demonstrate it, and in the two cases actually tested it was wrong. Any future gate on CF-194..CF-245 must rest on an INDEPENDENT grounding check performed at gate time against the cited summaries.md block or pdf_extract, not on this verification object and not on the blanket 'Text quality is good; a human gate can confirm it as is' clause that the 2026-08-29 revert appended to all 52 records.
